 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2024:000124 

 Dunne J. 

 Charleton J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 


 [2026] IESC 2 

 BETWEEN/ 

 GM 

 APPLICANT/APPELLANT 

 AND 

   

 IM 

 RESPONDENT 

 AND 

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 NOTICE PARTY 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Gerard Hogan delivered on the 23 rd day of  January 2026 

 

 1.       This appeal presents two important issues. First, do the Circuit Court and the District Court each have a jurisdiction to grant an Isaac Wunder order to prevent abusive litigation by a particular litigant? Second, if so, do the Circuit Court and the District Court each have a jurisdiction to grant an Isaac Wunder order which takes effect throughout the State and outside of the territorial limits of that court's jurisdiction? As the facts and the relevant legal issues have been comprehensively set out in the judgment of Dunne J., I can proceed immediately to address these issues. 

 The jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and the District Court to grant an Isaac Wunder order 

 2.        I entirely agree with the judgment which Dunne J. has just delivered to the effect that the Circuit Court and the District Court each enjoy such a jurisdiction in principle to grant Isaac Wunder orders. Article 34.1 of the Constitution vests the administration of justice in the judicial branch of government. As I pointed out in Kirwan v. Connors [2025] IESC 21 , this constitutional provision essentially designates the judiciary as the custodians of the administration of justice so that each court is obliged to ensure not only that the judicial process works efficiently and fairly, but also that this process is not used for oblique or abusive purposes. To that extent, it may be regarded as a regulation of the constitutional right of access to the courts which is also protected by Article 34.1 (read, if necessary, in conjunction with Article 40.3): see, for example, Murphy v. Greene [1990] 2 IR 566 at 578, where McCarthy J. referred to the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction in these terms. 

 3.       The making of an Isaac Wunder order accordingly serves the constitutional purposes which were identified in Kirwan v. Connors by ensuring that an abusive litigant cannot harass or oppress his opponent by repeated, fruitless litigation. While it may have been true a generation ago to say, as Costello J. did in O'Malley v. Irish Nationwide Building Society , High Court, 21st January 1984, that such an order would be made only "in very rare circumstances", this is, I think, no longer quite the case. These words were uttered in what were, perhaps, simpler times for the legal system. They came at a time when McCarthy J. could offer the view that it was doubtful "if the court records reveal many or even any instances of such officious interference" by abusive litigants: see Norris v. Attorney General [1984] IR 36 at 91. For whatever reason, oppressive litigation has, regrettably, become far more common since the mid-1980s. 

 4.       One way or another, therefore, I agree that the development of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction is a necessary and indispensable feature of the administration of justice so that these constitutionally derived powers must be deemed to be vested in both the Circuit Court and the District Court. I also agree with Collins J. that it would be desirable that the parameters of this jurisdiction were regulated by law. While it might be useful if this jurisdiction was regulated by statute law, it should, at a minimum, also be regulated by Rules of Court. 

 The local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and the District Court 

 5.       I now turn to the more difficult question in this appeal: can the Circuit Court or the District Court make an Isaac Wunder order with nationwide effect? (This is not an issue in the case of the High Court given that it enjoys a full original jurisdiction by virtue of Article 34.3.1⁰.) It is true that this Court has frequently observed in cases such as Grimes v. Owners of SS Bangor Bay [1948] IR 350 and The State (Boyle) v. Neylon [1986] IR 551 that the Circuit Court is one Court. It is nonetheless, like the District Court, also a court of local and limited jurisdiction for the purposes of Article 34.3.4⁰. While the courts have sometimes struggled to ascribe a fixed and consistent meaning to these constitutional requirements, nonetheless as Clarke C.J. observed in Permanent TSB plc v. Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 IR 375 at 397, a "real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited." 

 6.       In the context of the "local" requirement, this means that the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court must be bounded in some way by geographical considerations.  This does not mean that the hands of the Oireachtas are tied by reference to the considerations which governed the allocation of jurisdiction to the Circuit Court and District Court in 1937 or even in 1961 at the time of the enactment of the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961. The Oireachtas is, in principle, free to experiment in respect of the allocation of jurisdiction to the District and Circuit Courts. After all, Article 36.iii envisages that - subject, of course, to the requirements of Article 34 itself from which it may not derogate - the Oireachtas will legislate to regulate "the distribution of jurisdiction and business" of the courts. 

 7.       What it does mean, however, is that the Oireachtas must nonetheless respect the demarcation between the full original jurisdiction conferred on the High Court by Article 34.3.1⁰ on the one hand, and the "local and limited" nature of the Circuit Court's Article 34.3.4⁰ jurisdiction on the other. This means in turn that the latter Court "may not be erected into a localised replica of the High Court": see JP Casey, "The Constitution and the Legal System" (1979) 14 Irish Jurist 14 at 18. 

 8.       As matters stand, it is clear from the provisions of the Third Schedule to the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961, that jurisdiction is exercised locally, in that the Circuit Court can only hear cases against defendants residing in or carrying on business in or arising out of events happening in or immoveable property situate in, the Circuit in question.  But what is the status of these orders outside of the Circuit (or, in the case of the District Court, the relevant District) in which they are made? 

 9.       While it might be thought that there is a surprising dearth of authority on this point, it seems to me as a matter of principle that once the Circuit Court sitting in Circuit A has personal jurisdiction over a particular defendant (by reason, for example, of the fact that the defendant carries on business within that Circuit), it can then make an order in personam against that defendant, which can take effect outside of the jurisdiction of that Court. This simply reflects the complete nature of the personal jurisdiction which the Circuit Court enjoys over the defendant once these jurisdictional requirements specified in the 1961 Act have been satisfied. So, for example, if Circuit Court A makes a monetary award against a particular defendant, it would be entitled in principle to make a consequential Mareva -type order restraining that defendant from reducing his or her assets below a specified amount anywhere in the State (assuming, of course, that the substantive requirements of that Mareva jurisdiction have otherwise been satisfied). 

 10.   What the Circuit Court could not do, however, is to make an order in rem which takes effect outside of its jurisdiction. If, for example, the Circuit Court in Circuit A were to make a monetary award against X, it would not itself have jurisdiction to make a well-charging order against immoveable property situate in Circuit B in the event that this award remained undischarged. In those circumstances, it would be necessary to apply to the Circuit Court sitting in Circuit B for this relief. 

 11.    The reason for this distinction is that an in rem order of this kind applies indistinctly and indifferently to all persons and things who or which might be affected by its terms. If, for example, the Circuit Court were to make such a well-charging order in respect of immovable property situate outside of its Circuit, this would be tantamount to that Court acquiring a substantive jurisdiction to make orders in rem as against the entire world in respect of such property, which jurisdiction it would not otherwise possess. Not only has the Court not been given jurisdiction in respect of immoveable property situate outside of its own Circuit, but such an order might affect the rights of other persons not otherwise amenable to the jurisdiction of that Court. 

 12.    If one applies this principle to the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction at issue in the present case, it will be seen that the Circuit Court (and, by extension, the District Court) can make such an order in personam as against the offending litigant in respect of the litigation in which the Court has seisin, and in respect of which it already has personal jurisdiction over the party concerned. If, for example, X sues Y in Circuit Court A because this is the jurisdiction in which Y resides, then Circuit Court A can, where appropriate, make an Isaac Wunder order restraining X from suing Y in the Circuit Court anywhere in the State without prior leave. This, in essence, is the grant of ancillary relief to one of the parties in respect of litigation of which the court has jurisdiction and is properly seised. 

 13.    This jurisdiction does not, however, enable the Circuit Court to make an in rem Isaac Wunder order which would take effect generally in respect of other litigation and other parties outside of that particular Circuit. It could not, for instance, in the example I have just given, make an order which would restrain X from suing any other person in another Circuit without prior leave, since that would amount in substance to that Circuit Court exercising a general jurisdiction in respect of other parties and other litigation and in respect of parties and matters over which it does not enjoy such a jurisdiction. 

 Conclusions 

 14.   Subject to these observations, I agree with the judgment of Dunne J. that this appeal should be dismissed. I consider that the jurisdiction to make an Isaac Wunder order is ultimately derived from the courts' Article 34.1 obligation to conserve and protect the administration of justice. 

 15.   While the Circuit Court can in principle make an Isaac Wunder order in personam in respect of a party over which it has acquired personal jurisdiction which takes effect outside of that Circuit, that does not enable the Circuit Court to make an in rem Isaac Wunder order which would take effect generally outside of that Circuit which restrains that litigant from suing other parties in respect of which that Court does not have personal jurisdiction.
